entries.clue: Some artists use these small boat homes (6,4)

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels.
A ketch is a two-masted sailing boat.
A pad is slang for a home or flat.

annotation.surface: An idle remark about painters who live on little boats.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'small boat homes' sound like houseboats where artists live; split it into three separate words and the drawing books appear.
annotation.definitionFit: Sketch pads are the paper books artists draw in, so some artists use these.

entries.clue: Home match (4)

blocks.note: A house joined to its neighbour by one shared wall, in British shorthand.
The knockout round before the final, shortened.

annotation.walkthrough: Both senses are British short forms: a semi-detached house shares one wall with its neighbour, and a semi-final is the round before the final.
annotation.definitionFit: Semi is everyday British shorthand for both a semi-detached home and a semi-final match.

entries.clue: Nobleman seen in rear light (4)

indicatorNotes.seen in: Says the answer can be seen sitting inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: Drop the first R of rear and keep going into light for one letter: the run crosses the gap between the words.

annotation.walkthrough: Hidden words often straddle a word break, as here: r(EAR L)ight.
annotation.surface: A lord spotted in the glow of a car's rear light.
annotation.definitionFit: An earl is a British nobleman ranking just below a marquess.

entries.clue: Brook’s features (11)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Brook' is a verb (to tolerate), matching COUNTENANCE as a verb; 'features' is a plural noun for the singular noun, the face as a whole.

blocks.note: As a verb, to brook is to tolerate or allow, usually in 'brook no argument'.
A person's features taken together: their face and its expression.

annotation.surface: A remark about somebody named Brook and the look of their face.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital B dresses 'Brook' as a name, so ’s reads as possessive; in fact it is 'is', joining the verb brook to the noun features.
annotation.definitionFit: Countenance means both to tolerate (brook) and the face (features).

entries.clue: Informed of second loo, did you say? (5,2)

indicatorNotes.did you say?: Asks whether the words were heard rightly, so a sound, not a spelling, is wanted.

blocks.note: A privy is an old outdoor toilet; loo is British for toilet.
Second is number two; said out loud it is the same noise as TO.

annotation.surface: Someone checking they heard right about a second toilet.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads the clue out of order: loo first, then second, giving 'privy two', which is heard as the phrase meaning informed of.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: privy once meant private, so someone privy to a secret shares it and has been informed of it.

entries.clue: Initially didactic young lyricist (aged, now)? (5)

indicatorNotes.Initially: Take the opening letter of each of the words that follow.

blocks.note: Five words, so five letters: the head of each, read in order, ignoring the brackets.

annotation.surface: A potted biography of a preachy songwriter who has since grown old.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: Bob Dylan began as a young protest singer with lessons to teach, and he is an old man now.
annotation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan was the moralising young lyricist of 1960s protest songs, and is now in his eighties.

entries.clue: Somewhat eastwards, on and off (1,3)

indicatorNotes.on and off: Take one letter, skip one, and so on through the word.

blocks.note: e(A)s(T)w(A)r(D)s: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters.

annotation.walkthrough: 'On and off' sounds like the direction of travel is intermittent; it tells you to take the even letters and skip the odd ones.
annotation.surface: Travelling roughly east, but only intermittently.
annotation.definitionFit: A tad means a little, somewhat: 'a tad cold'.

entries.clue: Those two torture devices – for Spooner – they belong to bygone times (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a clause about things; THROWBACKS is the plural noun naming those things.

indicatorNotes.for Spooner: The Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the pair named here trade their fronts.

blocks.note: Those two are both; the word hands over its B and takes the R.
The rack stretched its victims; swap the R for the B and the word becomes BACKS.

annotation.surface: A grim aside that a pair of torture instruments are relics of the past.
annotation.walkthrough: The swap of B and R gives 'roth backs', and the first half only becomes THROW if its sounds are shuffled further, so this is a loose spoonerism: 'both racks' is the phrase to hear.
annotation.definitionFit: A throwback is something that recalls or belongs to an earlier era.

entries.clue: Soldiers run away: traitors! (6,4)

blocks.note: Soldiers who desert run away from their posts.
A rat is someone who betrays or informs on others.

annotation.surface: An officer's outburst as troops flee the field.
annotation.walkthrough: The Desert Rats were the British 7th Armoured Division, famous for fighting in North Africa in the Second World War.
annotation.definitionFit: The Desert Rats were British soldiers of the 7th Armoured Division.

entries.clue: Far-off beasts found in a Paris slum, upsetting (10)

indicatorNotes.upsetting: Knocking the letters over and out of order.

blocks.note: Ten letters to rearrange.

annotation.surface: Distant wild animals turning up in a poor Paris quarter, to everyone's distress.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Far-off' is doing real work: most marsupials, like kangaroos and koalas, live in Australia, about as far off as a British solver can go.
annotation.definitionFit: Marsupials, the pouched mammals, are chiefly found in faraway Australia.

entries.clue: Flower from flipping digital assistant (4)

indicatorNotes.flipping: Turn the word over so it reads back to front.

blocks.note: Siri is Apple's voice assistant.

annotation.surface: An annoyed user getting a flower from their voice assistant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word aimed at the gadget.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the iris, named for the Greek rainbow goddess, is one garden flower among many.

entries.clue: Force entertaining government to become re-elected (7,5)

indicatorNotes.entertaining: To entertain a guest is to have them inside, so one part holds another.

blocks.note: A re-elected party gets to stay in power.
G is the standard abbreviation for government.

annotation.surface: A political complaint about coercion used to win another term.
annotation.walkthrough: The G slips in between STAY IN and POWER. 'Force' is not compulsion here but strength, the kind that keeps going.
annotation.definitionFit: Staying power is endurance, the force that lets you last the course.

entries.clue: 20 isn’t one – but here it is! (5,6)

annotation.definition: 20 isn’t one – but here it is!

blocks.note: Read as the number twenty, this is true: it divides by 2, 4, 5 and 10.
Read as the grid reference 20 down, whose answer is THREE, the kind of number meant is one that divides only by itself and 1.

annotation.surface: A maths teacher's teasing remark that twenty both is and is not a certain kind of number.
annotation.walkthrough: '20' means two things: the number twenty, which has factors, and the grid entry 20 down, whose answer is THREE, a prime.
annotation.definitionFit: A prime number divides only by itself and one: twenty does not qualify, but three does.

entries.clue: After period of maturity, fruit and cheese finally rot (10)

indicatorNotes.After: Puts the next letters behind the first piece.
indicatorNotes.finally: Take the closing letter of each word it governs.

blocks.note: An adult era: the period of your life when you are mature.
fruiT, cheesE: the last letter of each.

annotation.surface: A note on letting fruit and cheese age until they spoil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Period of maturity' reads naturally as a food aging; parsed, it is ERA 'of' ADULT, written ADULT then ERA.
annotation.definitionFit: To adulterate is to spoil or corrupt something, as to rot is to make it go bad.

entries.clue: Everyman’s jokes? Of no significance (10)

blocks.note: The setter is Everyman, so 'Everyman is' is I'M from the setter's own mouth.
A comedian's jokes are their material.

annotation.surface: The setter running himself down: his jokes don't matter.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself means I or ME; here the ’s is 'is', so Everyman's becomes I'M.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what is immaterial has no bearing on the matter, as a lawyer might say of an objection.

entries.clue: Spotted something that includes good tenor performer (7)

indicatorNotes.that includes: The first thing takes the next letter inside it.

blocks.note: A domino is a tile marked with spots.
G is the standard abbreviation for good.

annotation.surface: Hunting for some spotty object that has a fine singer in it.
annotation.walkthrough: The G goes in before the final O: DOMIN(G)O. 'Spotted' looks like a verb meaning seen; it is an adjective, describing the spots on a domino.
annotation.definitionFit: Plácido Domingo is one of the most famous operatic tenors.

entries.clue: Flimsy song, a metaphor for nothing (4,3)

blocks.note: Something flimsy is thin.
An air is a tune or song.

annotation.surface: A critic dismissing a weak song as saying nothing at all.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'a metaphor for nothing' as a verdict on the song; it is the definition, as in 'vanished into thin air'.
annotation.definitionFit: Things that vanish into thin air disappear to nothing.

entries.clue: One’s starting out as initially low wage recipient (7)

annotation.definitionNote: 'One's starting out' is a clause (one who is starting out); LEARNER is the noun for that person.

indicatorNotes.initially: Take the opening letter of the next word.

blocks.note: The first letter of low.
Someone who receives a wage is an earner.

annotation.surface: A new starter on a poor wage.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a learner driver shows an L plate, which is why L so often means learner.
annotation.definitionFit: A learner is someone starting out, just beginning to acquire a skill.

entries.clue: Endlessly marketed daft insurance mascot? (7)

indicatorNotes.Endlessly: Cut the last letter off the next word.
indicatorNotes.daft: Silly, so the letters are jumbled.

blocks.note: Marketed without its final D.

annotation.surface: A sneer at a heavily advertised, silly company mascot.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain the price-comparison site Compare the Market advertises insurance with a cartoon meerkat; the question mark flags that a meerkat is only an example of such a mascot.
annotation.definitionFit: A cartoon meerkat is the famous mascot of a British insurance comparison website.

entries.clue: Second aggressive fellow’s punky hairdos (7)

blocks.note: A mo is a moment, a second: 'wait a mo'.
A hawk is someone who favours aggressive action; the ’s adds the S.

annotation.surface: A remark on the spiky hairstyles of a second tough guy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like an ordinal, the next fellow along; it is a noun, a brief moment, and 'hawk' is the political sense, the opposite of a dove.
annotation.definitionFit: A mohawk is the punk haircut with a single upright strip down the middle.

entries.clue: Oh, even Luther converted in final moments (8,4)

indicatorNotes.converted: Changed into another form, so the letters are rearranged.

blocks.note: Twelve letters to rearrange.

annotation.surface: Surprise that even Martin Luther underwent a deathbed conversion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Converted' fits the religious surface around Luther, which hides its job as an anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: The eleventh hour is the last possible moment.

entries.clue: Ether, quaint number (5)

indicatorNotes.quaint: Odd or peculiar, so the letters come out strangely arranged.

blocks.note: Five letters to rearrange.

annotation.surface: Ether as an old-fashioned figure, as a Victorian anaesthetic might seem.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Number' also teases 'anaesthetic' (something that numbs), which suits ether; here it is just a figure.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: three is one particular number, and the clue gives only the broad class.

entries.clue: Globalism overwhelming island (4)

indicatorNotes.overwhelming: The outer word engulfs the answer, holding it inside.

blocks.note: Skip the first three letters and the last two; the four in the middle are the island.

annotation.surface: Global culture swamping a small island.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a real complaint about tourism and globalisation swamping a holiday island, which is exactly where the answer sits: glo(BALI)sm.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Bali is one island of Indonesia, popular with tourists.

entries.clue: Island where you once sat next to small king (4)

indicatorNotes.once: Marks an old form of the word, no longer in everyday use.
indicatorNotes.sat next to: Places one piece beside the other.

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small.
K is king in chess notation.
Ye is the old word for you.

annotation.surface: An island where you once found yourself seated beside a minor monarch.
annotation.walkthrough: Skye is a large island off the west coast of Scotland; YE goes after S and K.
annotation.definitionFit: Skye is one of Scotland's Inner Hebrides islands.

entries.clue: Ill-natured help catching cold (4)

indicatorNotes.catching: One word catches the other and holds it inside.

blocks.note: Aid is help.
C is cold, as on a tap.

annotation.surface: A grumpy helper coming down with a cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Catching' reads as catching a cold; in the parse AID catches C: A(C)ID.
annotation.definitionFit: An acid remark or temper is sharp and ill-natured.

entries.clue: Fail to prepare to fire cartridge with no bullet (4,1,5)

blocks.note: You draw a gun from its holster to get ready to shoot.
A blank is a cartridge with powder but no bullet.

annotation.surface: A failure to get a gun ready for firing blanks.
annotation.walkthrough: The first 'to' is the link; the second belongs to 'prepare to fire'. Read literally, drawing a gun loaded with a blank is exactly what the phrase says.
annotation.definitionFit: To draw a blank is to fail to find or achieve what you were looking for.

entries.clue: Not quietly, removes skin from fish (4)

indicatorNotes.Not quietly: Quietly is P (piano in music), so remove the P.

blocks.note: To peel something is to remove its skin.
Drop the P from PEELS.

annotation.surface: Someone noisily skinning a fish.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'removes skin from fish' a kitchen task; the verb phrase is PEELS and fish is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Eels are long snake-like fish.

entries.clue: Wildly eviscerate group holding gunpowder? (3,7)

indicatorNotes.Wildly: Out of control, so the letters are thrown about.

blocks.note: Ten letters to rearrange.

annotation.surface: Violent talk of disembowelling a gang that is carrying explosives.
annotation.walkthrough: Gunpowder is a Chinese green tea rolled into little pellets, so a set of teapot and cups can hold it; the question mark flags the trick.
annotation.definitionFit: A tea service is a set of teapot, cups and saucers, which holds tea such as gunpowder.
